turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'm Sister Nkosi. I'll check your blood pressure before you go in, so just sit quiet for me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, sister. I don't know, is it bad again?
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Reading is one forty over eighty... ag, the cuff slipped. One fifty-six over ninety-two. Pulse is seventy-two.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Shame. I don't know what that means, doctor... sister.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Oxygen saturation ninety-six percent. Doctor's free, you can go through. He's in a bit of a rush this morning.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Sit. What's brought you in? Briefly.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. My feet, maybe. She talks for me.
[SEG0008] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm her daughter, I stay with her. Shoes don't fit by the afternoon, ankles quite puffy, and she's tired all the time.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long have the ankles been like that?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. I think. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0011] person_4 (CAREGIVER): It's a month. Since the long weekend, that's when I noticed the strap marks.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between two weeks and a month. Not exact. Short of breath?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Breathing is fine.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cough?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I don't think so.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain.
[SEG0020] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She gets puffed though. Even to the gate.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): You said the breathing was fine.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, well, actually, ja. If I walk to the robot I have to stop, I'm short of breath. I forget, doctor.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Since last week... no, more like three weeks. I don't know the day.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Dizzy when you stand up?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't get dizzy.
[SEG0027] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She does, hey. Yesterday by the kettle she grabbed the wall. She just won't say.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I wasn't dizzy. I just stood there.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Who packs the pill box?
[SEG0030] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I do. I live with her. Sometimes the Monday morning slot is still full when I get back from the shops, so I can't say she takes every dose.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): List them. Proper names if you can.
[SEG0032] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The water tablet is furosemide, forty milligrams in the morning. Then I also put the swelling tablet in at night. Might be the same one twice, I get muddled.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): It is the same tablet counted twice. Furosemide.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I thought the water one was twenty milligrams. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to pretend we know what went in. From tomorrow, furosemide forty milligrams, one tablet, mornings only. No second dose at night.
[SEG0036] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She takes Disprin as well, seventy-five milligrams... no, sorry, the hospital changed it to a hundred and fifty. One each morning.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): What else is in there?
[SEG0038] person_4 (CAREGIVER): A little white one at bedtime. Round, tiny. Label peeled off in my handbag. I wondered if it was the cholesterol tablet but I can't swear to it.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Just the little white one.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bring that bottle next time. Don't stop it blind.
[SEG0041] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The clinic doctor stopped the amlodipine. She was on five milligrams... no, it was ten, and he stopped the ten. That was about two months back, ankles were too fat.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any warfarin? Insulin? Other drops?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't know. I don't think there's more.
[SEG0044] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Eish, I left one out. Enalapril, ten milligrams in the morning, for the pressure. That's really the lot.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): File says heart failure and high blood pressure. Both still going?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. They say the heart is weak. The pressure has been there for years. I don't know, doctor, I just take what she gives me.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Shoes off. I'll look.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pitting oedema of both ankles, up to the malleoli. Calves are soft.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear, no crackles. Heart sounds are normal, no murmur.
[SEG0050] person_4 (CAREGIVER): While you're writing, the drive here was hectic, hey. Robot on William Nicol was out again.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Load shedding?
[SEG0052] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Ja, the robots were dead. We sat twenty minutes. Then my boy phoned about the cricket, the Proteas, can you believe that catch at midwicket.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): He plays soccer, my grandchild, not cricket. Little one, runs like a rabbit.
[SEG0054] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Under-ten, they had a friendly at the school. He wants new boots. I said after payday, not before.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): And the weather, shame, that wind this morning nearly took the washing.
[SEG0056] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Hot again by lunch though. Proper Highveld stuff. We were going to braai Saturday if the rain holds off.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Back to this. I'm calling it fluid retention, the heart failure not holding. That's my working impression, not final.
[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): Missed morning tablets could do the same thing. I can't separate the two yet.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I try.
[SEG0060] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cut the salt. No biltong, easy on the stock cubes and packet soup.
[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): Weigh yourself every morning, same scale, and tell your daughter the number.
[SEG0062] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll stand her on it and write the number down.
[SEG0063] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bloods today, urea and electrolytes, because of the water tablet and the kidneys. Sister can draw them on the way out.
[SEG0064] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the swelling is not down in a week, then a chest X-ray. Not today.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I come back?
[SEG0066] person_3 (DOCTOR): Book two weeks with me. Sooner only if she can't speak in sentences or the swelling shoots up.
[SEG0067] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll book at the desk. Two weeks.
[SEG0068] person_1 (NURSE): I heard bloods. I'll take her for the urea and electrolytes after this, if you're done.
[SEG0069] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ja, sister, today. That's the plan.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I still don't know half of it, hey.

spec.situation: Older patient with a live-in carer or daughter who manages the pill box; names of tablets are described ('the little white one', 'the water tablet'), one was stopped by another doctor, one is double-counted. Doctor reviews and changes one medicine.
features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

bad.reason: Provisional fluid retention from heart failure is stated; basis details like ankle swelling/known heart failure are implied, not explicitly cited.
bad.text: Fluid retention, with the heart failure not holding (certainty=provisional, basis=Ankle swelling, breathlessness, known heart failure and pitting oedema on examination, stated_by=doctor)

omissions.text: Negative finding asked and answered: patient initially denied shortness of breath ('No. Breathing is fine.') before later clarifying exertional shortness of breath.
Exertional shortness of breath detail is incomplete: patient has to stop when walking to the robot, and caregiver said she gets puffed even walking to the gate.
Medication adherence detail missing: caregiver said the Monday morning pill-box slot is sometimes still full when she gets back from the shops, so she cannot say the patient takes every dose.

Current furosemide use is recorded incompletely/wrongly: caregiver reported furosemide 40 mg in the morning and also said she had been putting what she thought was a 'swelling tablet' in at night, which the doctor clarified was the same tablet counted twice (duplicate furosemide night dose).

Amlodipine discontinuation timing/reason missing: clinic doctor stopped amlodipine about two months ago because the ankles were too swollen; dose history was uncertain between 5 mg and 10 mg, with caregiver finally saying he stopped the 10 mg.
Negative findings asked and answered but not recorded: patient denied warfarin, insulin, and other drops/medicines when specifically asked.
Plan detail missing: bloods are to be done today on the way out by the nurse/sister.
